pack.title: Elasticity of Demand and Supply
pack.summary: This pack explains how strongly buyers and sellers respond to changes in price and income. It covers price elasticity of demand and how to calculate it, what makes demand elastic or inelastic, how elasticity affects total revenue, income and cross elasticity, and price elasticity of supply, all with Nigerian examples such as petrol, bread, danfo fares and Lagos food markets.

sections.title: What elasticity measures
sections.explanation:
Elasticity measures how much one variable responds when another changes. In economics we mostly ask: if the price of a good changes by 1%, by what percentage does the quantity bought or sold change?

We use percentages, not raw numbers, so we can compare very different goods. A ₦50 rise means a lot for a ₦100 sachet of pure water but very little for a ₦50,000 bag of rice. Percentages remove the units.

Price elasticity of demand (PED) is the most common measure. Because price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions (the law of demand), PED is negative, but economists usually talk about its absolute value.

keyTerms.definition: The responsiveness of one variable (e.g. quantity) to a change in another (e.g. price), measured in percentage terms.
% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.
'All other things being equal': only the price changes while income, tastes and other prices stay fixed.
The size of a number ignoring its sign; PED of −2 has an absolute value of 2.

sections.workedExample:
A Yaba bakery raises the price of a loaf from ₦1,000 to ₦1,100 (a 10% rise). Daily sales fall from 500 to 450 loaves (a 10% fall).
PED = −10% ÷ 10% = −1, so |PED| = 1.
This is unit elastic: quantity changed by the same percentage as price.

sections.title: Calculating PED and the midpoint method
sections.explanation:
The simple formula divides the percentage change in quantity by the percentage change in price. The problem is that the answer changes depending on whether price goes up or down, because each percentage uses a different starting point.

The midpoint (arc) method fixes this by using the average of the old and new values as the base:
% change in Q = (Q2 − Q1) ÷ ((Q1 + Q2) ÷ 2) × 100, and the same for price.

Interpreting the result: |PED| > 1 is elastic, |PED| < 1 is inelastic, |PED| = 1 is unit elastic. The extreme cases are perfectly inelastic (0, a vertical demand curve) and perfectly elastic (infinite, a horizontal demand curve).

keyTerms.definition: Calculates percentage changes using the average of the start and end values, so the answer is the same in both directions.
|PED| > 1: quantity demanded changes by a larger percentage than price.
|PED| < 1: quantity demanded changes by a smaller percentage than price.
PED = 0: quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes.
PED is infinite: any price rise makes quantity demanded fall to zero.

sections.workedExample:
Danfo fares on a route rise from ₦400 to ₦600, and daily riders fall from 1,000 to 800.
Midpoint % change in Q = (800 − 1,000) ÷ 900 × 100 = −22.2%.
Midpoint % change in P = (600 − 400) ÷ 500 × 100 = 40%.
PED = −22.2 ÷ 40 = −0.56, so |PED| = 0.56: demand is inelastic. Most commuters have no cheaper way to get to work.

sections.title: Determinants of price elasticity of demand
sections.explanation:
Several factors decide whether demand is elastic or inelastic.

1. Availability of close substitutes: the more substitutes, the more elastic. One brand of noodles is elastic because buyers can switch brands; noodles as a whole are less elastic.
2. Necessity vs luxury: necessities such as petrol, kerosene and basic food are inelastic; luxuries such as eating out are more elastic.
3. Share of income: goods that take a big share of the budget (rent, school fees) are more elastic than cheap items like salt or matches.
4. Time period: demand becomes more elastic over time because people find alternatives.
5. Definition of the market: narrowly defined goods are more elastic than broad categories.

keyTerms.definition: A good that can be used in place of another, e.g. garri instead of bread.
A good people keep buying even when the price rises; usually inelastic.
In the short run buyers can't easily change habits; in the long run they adjust, so demand becomes more elastic.

sections.workedExample:
After the 2023 petrol subsidy removal, pump prices roughly tripled, but most okada riders and commuters still had to buy fuel the next week: short-run demand was inelastic.
Over the following months some people switched to CNG buses, walked short trips, carpooled or moved closer to work, so the same price rise cut quantity demanded by more: long-run demand became more elastic.

sections.title: Elasticity and total revenue
sections.explanation:
Total revenue (TR) = price × quantity sold. Elasticity tells a seller what happens to TR when they change price.

If demand is elastic, raising the price lowers TR, because the fall in quantity outweighs the higher price. Cutting the price raises TR.
If demand is inelastic, raising the price raises TR, because quantity falls only a little. Cutting the price lowers TR.
If demand is unit elastic, TR stays the same.

This is why governments tax inelastic goods like fuel, tobacco and alcohol: sales fall only slightly, so tax revenue is large and reliable.

keyTerms.definition: Price × quantity sold; equal to total spending by buyers on the good.
Using the direction of TR after a price change to tell whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
Who actually bears a tax; buyers bear more of a tax when demand is inelastic.

sections.workedExample:
A suya seller in Surulere charges ₦2,000 a stick and sells 100 sticks a night: TR = ₦200,000.
She raises the price to ₦2,500 and sales fall to 60 sticks: TR = ₦150,000.
TR fell after a price rise, so demand is elastic (there are many other suya spots nearby). She should not raise her price.

sections.title: Income, cross and supply elasticity
sections.explanation:
Income elasticity of demand (YED) = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. If YED is positive the good is normal; if it is greater than 1 it is a luxury. If YED is negative the good is inferior: people buy less of it as they get richer.

Cross elasticity of demand (XED) = % change in quantity demanded of good A ÷ % change in price of good B. Positive XED means substitutes; negative XED means complements; zero means unrelated.

Price elasticity of supply (PES) = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price. Supply is more elastic when producers have spare capacity, stocks, easy access to inputs and more time. Farm produce is inelastic in the short run because crops take months to grow.

keyTerms.definition: % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income.
A good with negative YED: demand falls as income rises.
% change in quantity demanded of one good ÷ % change in price of another.
Goods used together (negative XED), e.g. generators and petrol.
% change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price.

sections.workedExample:
A student's monthly allowance rises from ₦50,000 to ₦60,000 (a 20% rise). Their weekly spending on eating out rises from 2 meals to 3 (a 50% rise): YED = 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, a luxury.
Over the same period they buy fewer sachets of garri, from 10 to 8 (a −20% change): YED = −20 ÷ 20 = −1, an inferior good for this student.

questions.question: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
options: How much total revenue changes when price changes
How responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price
How responsive supply is to a change in income
The slope of the supply curve
questions.modelAnswer: How responsive quantity demanded is to a change in price.
questions.explanation: PED compares the % change in quantity demanded with the % change in price.

questions.question: Why do economists use percentage changes to measure elasticity?
options: They remove units so different goods can be compared
questions.modelAnswer: Percentages remove units so different goods can be compared.
questions.explanation: A ₦50 change means very different things for pure water and rice; percentages make them comparable.

questions.question: Price elasticity of demand is usually negative because…
options: of the law of demand: price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
questions.modelAnswer: Because of the law of demand.
questions.explanation: When price rises, quantity demanded falls, so the ratio of the two % changes is negative.

questions.question: In your own words, what does 'ceteris paribus' mean when we calculate elasticity?
questions.modelAnswer: It means 'all other things being equal': we assume only the price changes, while income, tastes and the prices of other goods stay the same.
questions.explanation: Holding other factors fixed lets us isolate the effect of price on quantity.

questions.question: Bread rises from ₦1,000 to ₦1,100 and sales fall from 500 to 450 loaves. What is |PED| using simple percentages?
questions.explanation: Quantity falls 10% and price rises 10%, so 10 ÷ 10 = 1 (unit elastic).

questions.question: Demand is called elastic when |PED| is…
questions.modelAnswer: Greater than 1.
questions.explanation: Elastic means quantity responds by a larger percentage than price.

questions.question: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is…
questions.modelAnswer: Vertical.
questions.explanation: Quantity demanded does not change whatever the price, so the curve is vertical (PED = 0).

questions.question: Why is the midpoint (arc) method preferred to the simple percentage formula?
options: It always gives a bigger answer
It gives the same elasticity whether price rises or falls
questions.modelAnswer: It gives the same answer in both directions.
questions.explanation: Using the average of the start and end values as the base removes the direction problem.

questions.question: Danfo fares rise from ₦400 to ₦600 and riders fall from 1,000 to 800. Using the midpoint method, |PED| is about…
questions.modelAnswer: About 0.56.

questions.question: If |PED| = 0.4, demand is…
questions.modelAnswer: Inelastic.
questions.explanation: Any value between 0 and 1 is inelastic.

questions.question: The price of a sachet of pure water rises from ₦50 to ₦70 and daily sales at a stall fall from 200 to 180. Using the midpoint method, calculate PED and say whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
questions.explanation: Quantity fell by a much smaller percentage than price rose.

questions.question: Describe what a perfectly elastic demand curve looks like and what it means for a seller.
questions.modelAnswer: It is a horizontal line. If the seller raises their price even slightly above the market price, quantity demanded falls to zero, because buyers switch to identical sellers.
questions.explanation: Perfect elasticity happens with identical products and many sellers, like one trader among many selling the same tomatoes.

questions.question: Which of these is likely to have the MOST elastic demand?
options: One particular brand of instant noodles
questions.modelAnswer: One particular brand of instant noodles.
questions.explanation: A single brand has many close substitutes, so buyers switch easily when its price rises.

questions.question: Demand usually becomes more elastic over time because…
options: buyers find substitutes and change habits
questions.modelAnswer: Buyers find substitutes and change habits.
questions.explanation: Given time, people switch to CNG buses, carpool, change diets and so on.

questions.question: A good that takes up a large share of a household's income tends to have demand that is…
questions.modelAnswer: More elastic.
questions.explanation: A price rise on a big budget item (like rent) is felt strongly, so buyers respond more.

questions.question: Why was demand for petrol inelastic right after the subsidy removal?
options: It is a necessity with few short-run alternatives
Incomes rose at the same time
questions.modelAnswer: It is a necessity with few short-run alternatives.
questions.explanation: Commuters and okada riders still had to buy fuel in the short run.

questions.question: 'Food' as a whole has less elastic demand than 'jollof rice at Mama Put X' because…
options: broad categories have fewer substitutes than narrowly defined goods
questions.modelAnswer: Broad categories have fewer substitutes.
questions.explanation: You can switch from one Mama Put to another, but there is no substitute for food in general.

questions.question: List three factors that make demand for a good more elastic.
questions.modelAnswer: Many close substitutes; the good is a luxury rather than a necessity; it takes a large share of income; and a longer time period to adjust (any three).
questions.explanation: These all make it easier or more worthwhile for buyers to cut back when price rises.

questions.question: Using petrol in Nigeria as an example, explain the difference between short-run and long-run elasticity of demand.
questions.modelAnswer: In the short run, demand for petrol is inelastic because people still need to get to work and have no quick alternative. In the long run it becomes more elastic as people switch to CNG buses, carpool, walk short trips or move closer to work, so the same price rise reduces quantity demanded by more.
questions.explanation: Time lets buyers find substitutes and change habits.

questions.question: If demand is elastic and a seller raises the price, total revenue will…
questions.modelAnswer: Fall.
questions.explanation: The percentage fall in quantity is bigger than the percentage rise in price.

questions.question: If demand is inelastic, which pricing move raises total revenue?
questions.modelAnswer: Raising the price.
questions.explanation: Quantity falls only a little, so price × quantity goes up.

questions.question: A suya seller raises her price from ₦2,000 to ₦2,500 and sales fall from 100 to 60 sticks. What happens to total revenue?
questions.modelAnswer: It falls from ₦200,000 to ₦150,000.

questions.question: Governments often tax fuel, tobacco and alcohol heavily because demand for them is…
questions.modelAnswer: Inelastic.
questions.explanation: Sales fall only slightly, so tax revenue is large and predictable.

questions.question: When demand is unit elastic, a 10% price cut makes total revenue…
questions.modelAnswer: Stay the same.
questions.explanation: Quantity rises by the same percentage as price falls, so TR is unchanged.

questions.question: Explain the total revenue test and how a trader can use it to tell whether demand for her goods is elastic.
questions.modelAnswer: She changes her price and watches total revenue (price × quantity). If she raises the price and TR falls (or cuts the price and TR rises), demand is elastic. If TR moves in the same direction as price, demand is inelastic. If TR doesn't change, demand is unit elastic.
questions.explanation: The direction of TR after a price change reveals elasticity without calculating PED.

questions.question: A good with negative income elasticity of demand is called…
questions.modelAnswer: An inferior good.
questions.explanation: Demand falls as income rises.

questions.question: If the price of generators rises and the quantity of petrol demanded falls, cross elasticity of demand is…
questions.modelAnswer: Negative: they are complements.
questions.explanation: Generators and petrol are used together, so a price rise for one lowers demand for the other.

questions.question: A student's allowance rises 20% and spending on eating out rises 50%. YED is…
questions.modelAnswer: 2.5: a luxury.
questions.explanation: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, which is positive and greater than 1.

questions.question: Why is the supply of tomatoes inelastic in the short run?
options: Farmers can't grow more instantly: crops take months
questions.modelAnswer: Crops take months to grow, so farmers can't increase output quickly.
questions.explanation: PES is low when production takes time and stocks can't be stored long.

questions.question: Explain the difference between substitutes and complements using cross elasticity of demand, with one Nigerian example of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Substitutes have positive XED: when the price of one rises, demand for the other rises (e.g. bread and garri, or bus and okada rides). Complements have negative XED: when the price of one rises, demand for the other falls (e.g. generators and petrol, or cars and fuel).
questions.explanation: The sign of XED shows how two goods are related.

questions.question: Give two reasons why a factory with spare capacity has more elastic supply than one running at full capacity.
questions.modelAnswer: With spare capacity it can quickly raise output when the price rises, using idle machines and workers, without big extra costs. A factory at full capacity would need to build new plant or hire and train staff, which takes time and money, so its supply responds less.
questions.explanation: Spare capacity and easy access to inputs make PES higher.
